title: Scabies, including crusted scabies
subject: rheumatology-dermatology
setting: Primary care, dermatology, hospitals and care institutions
summary: Treat the patient and all close contacts at the same time with permethrin 5% cream left on for 8 to 12 hours and repeated after 7 to 14 days, or oral ivermectin 200 mcg/kg with food as 2 doses 1 week apart. Crusted scabies needs combined topical and repeated oral ivermectin with isolation.

sections.title: Recognise
items: Intense generalised itch, worse at night, starting 3 to 6 weeks after a first infestation (1 to 3 days after re-infestation), often with itchy household contacts.

Burrows and papules on finger webs, wrists, elbows, axillae, periumbilical skin, waistline, buttocks and genitals (penile and scrotal nodules are highly suggestive) and areolae. Infants often have palm, sole, face and scalp lesions with vesicles or pustules.

Crusted scabies: thick hyperkeratotic crusted plaques (hands, feet, nails, scalp, bony prominences) with little itch and huge mite numbers; highly contagious. Occurs with HIV, HTLV-1, immunosuppressants, older age, disability or neurological disease.

Complications: secondary impetigo and cellulitis (Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes) and sepsis; in endemic settings, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis and possibly rheumatic heart disease.

sections.title: Diagnosis and testing
items: Diagnosis is mainly clinical (2020 IACS consensus criteria). Confirm when possible by dermoscopy (delta or jet-with-contrail sign) or microscopy of skin scrapings (mites, eggs, faeces); a negative scraping does not exclude scabies.
Screen sexually active adults for other sexually transmitted infections, including HIV (IUSTI).
Crusted scabies: check HIV and, where relevant, HTLV-1 serology and CBC; review immunosuppressive drugs.
Swab infected lesions and treat secondary bacterial infection.

sections.title: Classic scabies
items: Treat the patient and all household, close and sexual contacts at the same time, even without symptoms (IUSTI: contacts in the past 2 months; CDC: in the past month).

Permethrin 5% cream (first line; from 2 months of age; safe in pregnancy and breastfeeding): apply at night to cool, dry skin of the whole body, including finger and toe webs, under nails, genitals and navel, and the scalp, face and ears in infants, young children and older people; wash off after 8 to 12 hours; repeat after 7 to 14 days.
Reapply to the hands if they are washed during the treatment period.

Oral ivermectin 200 mcg/kg with food, 2 doses 1 week apart (IUSTI; CDC 7 to 14 days): useful for institutions, extensive disease or when topical treatment is impractical. Labelled not for children under 15 kg or pregnancy.

Alternatives: benzyl benzoate 25% lotion (adults) on 2 consecutive nights, repeated after 7 days, diluted for children; precipitated sulphur 6 to 10% ointment on 3 successive nights (infants under 2 months, pregnancy).
Wash clothing, bedding and towels used in the 3 days before treatment at 50 degrees C or more and dry hot, or seal them in a plastic bag for at least 72 hours (CDC) to 1 week (IUSTI).
Itch: emollients, a mild topical corticosteroid and a sedating antihistamine at night. Post-scabetic itch and nodules can last 2 to 4 weeks and do not mean treatment failure.

sections.title: Crusted scabies
items: Manage with specialist input, usually admitted: contact precautions (gloves and gowns), single room, and treatment of all contacts and exposed staff.

Combine topical and oral treatment: permethrin 5% (or benzyl benzoate 25%) daily for 7 days then twice weekly until cure, plus ivermectin 200 mcg/kg on days 1, 2 and 8; severe cases add days 9 and 15, or days 9, 15, 22 and 29.
Keratolytic cream (for example urea 10% or salicylic acid 5%) between permethrin applications to remove crusts; trim nails and treat beneath them.
Rigorous environmental cleaning (vacuum furniture and carpets, launder all fabrics); treat secondary infection and look for sepsis.

sections.title: Special groups and outbreaks
items: Infants under 2 months: sulphur ointment or specialist advice; permethrin is licensed from 2 months. Use mittens to limit hand-to-mouth transfer of cream.

Pregnancy and breastfeeding: permethrin first line (wash off the nipple area before feeds and reapply after); benzyl benzoate and sulphur are alternatives; ivermectin is generally avoided in pregnancy.

Care homes, hostels and hospital wards: treat all residents and staff at the same time, often with oral ivermectin, and involve infection control. WHO supports mass drug administration with 2 doses of ivermectin where community prevalence is 10% or more.
Ivermectin may raise the INR with warfarin; use caution in severe liver disease.

sections.title: Follow-up
items: Review 2 weeks after completing treatment (IUSTI). Cure: no active lesions or nocturnal itch 1 week after the end of treatment; new burrows or lesions after 2 to 4 weeks suggest failure or reinfestation.

Most failures come from incomplete application (ankles, toe webs and sacrum are often missed), a missed second application or untreated contacts; true permethrin tolerance has been reported in some regions.
Avoid close contact until the patient and partners have completed treatment; children can usually return to school the day after the first treatment.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Treating only the index patient, so untreated contacts reinfest the household.
Mistaking scabies for eczema or urticaria and giving topical steroid alone, which masks and spreads it.
Missing crusted scabies in an older, immunosuppressed or institutionalised patient with scaly crusts and little itch: the usual source of outbreaks.
Repeated scabicide for persistent post-scabetic itch, causing irritant dermatitis.
Using lindane, which is no longer recommended because of neurotoxicity.

drugs.name: Permethrin 5% cream
drugs.dose: Apply to the whole body (up to 30 g for an adult), leave 8 to 12 hours, then wash off; repeat after 7 to 14 days
drugs.notes: First line from 2 months of age; safe in pregnancy and breastfeeding.

drugs.name: Ivermectin (oral)
drugs.dose: 200 mcg/kg orally with food as 2 doses 1 week apart; crusted scabies: days 1, 2 and 8 (plus 9 and 15, or 9, 15, 22 and 29 if severe)
drugs.notes: Labelled not for children under 15 kg or pregnancy. May raise INR with warfarin.

drugs.name: Benzyl benzoate 25% lotion
drugs.dose: Adults: apply to the whole body at night on 2 consecutive nights, repeat after 7 days
drugs.notes: Irritant. Dilute for children and further for infants. Alternative topical for crusted scabies.

drugs.name: Precipitated sulphur 6 to 10% ointment
drugs.dose: Apply to the whole body on 3 successive nights
drugs.notes: Option for infants under 2 months and pregnancy; messy with an odour.
